model.name: AI Agent
model.purpose: Govern an autonomous computational actor that senses and responds to an environment, holds identity, delegated authority, tools, memory and policy, and can be discovered, constrained, evaluated and retired independently of storage format or access interface.
model.scope_statement: This meta-model covers a single AI agent as a durable actor record: who it is, what it is allowed to do, which skills and tools it may use, how it is remembered and constrained, how it is registered and life-cycled on a platform, how it relates to systems, persons, prompts and runs, and which evidence is required to operate it. Semantics are format-neutral; JSON, YAML, Agent Cards, MCP messages, Git and databases are projections.
in_scope: Agent identifiers, names, locators and discovery manifests
Autonomy classification, goals, delegated authority and human-oversight gates
Skill catalogs, tool and resource bindings, and agent-grain memory architecture
Platform lifecycle, directory registration, lease, mobility and decommission
Ownership, provider and deployer roles, access, audit and retention
Protocol alignments for inter-agent communication and tool invocation
Evaluation, provenance and threat-posture evidence attached to the agent record
out_of_scope: The enclosing AI system as a whole (WM-AI-001), including system-level risk management and model cards
A single agent run, task, conversation or execution trace (WM-AI-004)
Prompt templates and agent configuration documents as first-class instruction artifacts (WM-AI-005)
Natural-person legal personality and civil identity (WM-PER-003), except as owner or principal references
Foundation-model weights, training corpora and model-provider catalogs as such
Physical robot embodiment, kinematics and actuator control
Storage engines, wire encodings, Git, MCP transports, MongoDB collections or operator UIs as semantics

boundary_notes.distinction: ISO/IEC 22989 distinguishes an AI agent (an automated entity that senses, responds and acts toward goals) from an AI system (an engineered system that generates outputs for human-defined objectives). This model records the actor; the parent system, its components and system lifecycle remain WM-AI-001.

A2A treats a Task as a stateful unit of work with SUBMITTED/WORKING/COMPLETED (and related) states; FIPA treats the agent process lifecycle separately (initiated, active, suspended, waiting, transit). This model holds the durable actor; runs, tasks and traces are sibling execution records.

Operational instructions, system prompts and configuration documents are referenced by an agent; they are not the agent. A2A Agent Cards describe identity, skills and interfaces without exposing internal instructions; MCP treats prompts as a server feature distinct from the host agent.

FIPA requires an agent to have at least one owner and a distinguishable identity; the EU AI Act assigns legal duties to providers and deployers, not to the agent. The agent is never a natural or legal person in this model.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 22989:2022 Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology
sources.relevance: Normative definition of AI agent (3.1.1) as an automated entity that senses and responds to its environment and takes actions to achieve its goals; distinguishes agents from AI systems, components and human-defined objectives; supplies shared vocabulary for autonomy-related properties.

sources.title: FIPA Agent Management Specification SC00023J
sources.relevance: Normative agent platform reference model: Agent Identifier (immutable name, addresses, resolvers), mandatory owner, AMS/DF/MTS, lifecycle states and transitions, registration/lease, directory search, and management functions register/deregister/modify/search/get-description.

sources.title: FIPA ACL Message Structure Specification SC00061G
sources.relevance: Normative inter-agent message parameters: performative, sender, receiver, reply-to, content, language, encoding, ontology, protocol, conversation-id, reply-with, in-reply-to and reply-by; globally unique conversation identifiers.

sources.title: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification, Version 1.0.0
sources.relevance: Current open inter-agent protocol: Agent Card identity, skills, interfaces, security schemes, capabilities, opaque execution (peers do not receive internal state, memory or tools), task operations, extended authenticated cards, and well-known discovery.

sources.title: Model Context Protocol Specification (2026-07-28) and Tools
sources.relevance: Normative host/client/server model for exposing tools, resources and prompts to LLM applications; tool identity, schemas, list/call, consent and human-in-the-loop expectations, untrusted annotations, and tool-safety requirements.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), consolidated
sources.relevance: Legal definition of an AI system as a machine-based system with varying levels of autonomy; provider and deployer roles; territorial scope for placing on the market and use; agent actors inherit operator duties from the system they instantiate rather than becoming legal persons.

sources.title: NIST AI 800-2 Initial Public Draft: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models
sources.organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST CAISI)
sources.relevance: Defines agent scaffolding as how a model is turned into an agent (for example ReAct or pre-built agent products), distinguishes inference, scaffolding and task settings, and requires explicit agent budgets and stopping conditions for agentic evaluation.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 and Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations v1.1
sources.organization: OWASP Foundation / Gen AI Security Project (Agentic Security Initiative)
sources.version_or_date: Top 10 2026 (December 2025); Threats and Mitigations v1.1 December 2025
sources.relevance: Peer-reviewed agentic threat taxonomy and Top 10 for autonomous applications that plan and act with tools: memory poisoning, goal manipulation, tool misuse, and the requirement to treat autonomy, authority, tool access and memory as first-class risk surfaces.

bundles.name: Identity, naming and discovery
bundles.description: How an agent is uniquely named, distinguished from other agents, classified by kind and autonomy, and published for discovery without treating locators as storage formats.
bundles.rationale: FIPA makes a globally unique immutable AID name the identity kernel and requires directory registration; A2A publishes a self-describing Agent Card at a well-known locator; ISO/IEC 22989 supplies the typed concept AI agent. Without this bundle an operator cannot tell which actor is present.

layers.name: Master identity and name equality
layers.description: Authoritative identifiers, display names, version of the agent software, and rules for identity equivalence and immutability.

findings.name: Agent master identity
findings.description: The durable identity of an agent is a master-system identifier, typically the FIPA AID name on the home agent platform, optionally accompanied by a governed IRI or Dimension-assigned UUID/ULID. FIPA treats two AIDs as equivalent when their name parameters match and forbids changing the name during the agent's lifetime; addresses and resolvers may change. A2A separately records a human-readable name, description and agent version on the Agent Card. A date is not an identifier.

questions.text: What authoritative master-system identifier does the home Agent Management System or adopting platform assign to this agent?
Under which equality rule are two agent records treated as the same actor, and is the primary name immutable for the agent's lifetime?
What human-readable name, description and agent software version are published for operators and peer agents?
What governed global IRI, well-known locator or Dimension UUID/ULID is recorded when no platform AID is available or when cross-domain discovery is required?

data_elements.name: Master-system agent identifier
data_elements.description: Globally unique name issued by the AMS or home platform, corresponding to FIPA AID name.

data_elements.name: Transport addresses
data_elements.description: Ordered locators at which the agent can be contacted; order implies preference.

data_elements.name: Name resolvers
data_elements.description: Sequence of AIDs that can resolve this agent to transport addresses.

data_elements.name: Display name
data_elements.description: Human-readable name as in an A2A Agent Card.

data_elements.name: Agent software version
data_elements.description: Version of this agent implementation, distinct from protocol version.

artifacts.name: Agent identifier record
artifacts.description: Canonical identity object holding master-system id, aliases, addresses, resolvers, display metadata and version.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by master-system agent identifier (FIPA AID name); Dimension UUID only if the platform issues none.

layers.name: Discovery manifests and classification
layers.description: How an agent advertises itself and how it is classified by kind, autonomy and capability without implying a particular encoding.

findings.name: Discovery manifest and locators
findings.description: A2A requires a self-describing Agent Card covering identity, capabilities, skills, interfaces and authentication, commonly retrieved from a well-known URI. FIPA Directory Facilitators provide yellow-pages service descriptions. Extended cards may be released only after authentication. Locators are identifiers plus access hints, not the storage format.

questions.text: Where is this agent's discovery manifest published, and which protocol bindings, tenants and protocol versions does it advertise?
Does the agent offer an authenticated extended discovery card, and which additional skills or interfaces appear only after authentication?
Which optional interaction capabilities (streaming, push notifications, extensions) does the agent declare, and how are undeclared capabilities rejected?
Which default input and output media types does the agent accept across skills?

data_elements.name: Discovery manifest locator
data_elements.description: URI or directory key where the Agent Card or DF description is obtained.

data_elements.name: Supported interfaces
data_elements.description: Ordered list of interface locators with protocol binding, protocol version and optional tenant.

data_elements.name: Security schemes
data_elements.description: Declared authentication and authorization schemes for contacting the agent.

data_elements.name: Declared capabilities
data_elements.description: Boolean and extension capability set from the discovery manifest.

artifacts.name: Agent discovery card
artifacts.description: Self-describing manifest of identity, skills, interfaces, capabilities and security requirements, independent of JSON-versus-protobuf encoding.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Identified by agent master-system id plus manifest version; well-known locator is a secondary key.

findings.name: Kind and autonomy class
findings.description: ISO/IEC 22989 defines an AI agent as an automated entity that senses, responds and acts toward goals. The EU AI Act defines AI systems as machine-based systems designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy; it does not create a separate legal class 'agent'. Classification therefore records agent kind, autonomy band, and whether the actor is a platform service (AMS/DF) or an application agent, as alignment rather than EU conformance.

questions.text: Does this actor meet the ISO/IEC 22989 definition of an AI agent, and if not, which neighbouring concept (AI system, AI component, non-agent software) applies?
What declared autonomy band does this agent operate in, relative to varying autonomy in the EU AI Act definition and any human denial rights over tool use?
Is this agent an application actor or a reserved platform service such as AMS or DF, and which reserved AID pattern does it use?

data_elements.name: Agent kind code
data_elements.description: Classification of the actor against ISO agent versus system/component and FIPA application versus platform service.

data_elements.name: Autonomy band
data_elements.description: Declared autonomy level of the agent as an actor, aligned to EU 'varying levels of autonomy' without claiming a statutory agent class.

data_elements.name: Task-scope class
data_elements.description: Whether the agent is scoped to a bounded task family or advertised as broadly capable; treated as an operational class, not a claim of general intelligence.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Classification codes, definition matches and autonomy bands are inline governed values on the agent record. They are not a separate serial artifact; evidence of the classification decision is attached under evaluation-evidence.

bundles.name: Goals, authority and policy
bundles.description: What the agent is trying to achieve, what authority it may exercise on behalf of a principal, which human gates apply, and which constraints and threat controls bound its action.
bundles.rationale: ISO agents act to achieve goals; FIPA requires ownership; MCP requires user consent and a human ability to deny tool invocations; OWASP treats goal manipulation, tool misuse and memory poisoning as first-class agentic threats. Authority is not implied by identity.

layers.name: Goals and delegated authority
layers.description: Goal sets, success criteria, mandates, permission scopes and human-oversight gates attached to the agent rather than to a single run.

findings.name: Goals and success criteria
findings.description: An ISO AI agent takes actions to achieve its goals. Goal statements, in-scope objectives, explicit out-of-scope objectives and measurable success or stop criteria belong on the agent record so that goal hijack can be detected against a baseline. Run-specific tasks remain WM-AI-004.

questions.text: What standing goals and in-scope objectives is this agent authorised to pursue?
Which objectives are explicitly out of scope, and which stop or success criteria terminate pursuit of a goal?
Who may change the agent's goal set, and what evidence is required before a goal mutation is accepted?

data_elements.name: Primary goals
data_elements.description: Standing goal statements the agent is authorised to pursue.

data_elements.name: Success and stop criteria
data_elements.description: Measurable conditions under which pursuit of a goal succeeds or must stop.

data_elements.name: Goal owner reference
data_elements.description: Person or organisation accountable for the declared goals.

artifacts.name: Agent goal charter
artifacts.description: Serial statement of authorised goals, exclusions and success criteria against which goal-manipulation checks are made.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by agent master-system id plus charter version.

findings.name: Delegated authority and oversight
findings.description: FIPA requires at least one owner. MCP requires explicit user consent before tool invocation and states there should always be a human in the loop able to deny tool calls. The EU AI Act places duties on providers and deployers of autonomous AI systems. This finding records the mandate, permission scopes, spend or action limits, and oversight mode of the agent as a delegated actor, not as a legal person.

questions.text: On whose behalf may this agent act, and what mandate or permission scopes are delegated to it?
Which quantitative or categorical limits bound the agent's autonomous actions, including tool classes it may never invoke?
Which operations require prior human consent or allow in-loop denial, and what happens if the human is unavailable?
When was the current mandate granted, last reviewed, suspended or revoked, and at what observation time was that recorded?

data_elements.name: Principal reference
data_elements.description: Owner or user on whose behalf the agent acts.

data_elements.name: Permission scopes
data_elements.description: Delegated action and data scopes, including tool and resource classes.

data_elements.name: Human denial flag
data_elements.description: Whether a human can deny tool invocations before execution.

data_elements.name: Mandate state
data_elements.description: Granted, suspended, expired or revoked.

artifacts.name: Delegation mandate
artifacts.description: Instrument recording principal, scopes, limits, consent rules and validity interval.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by mandate identifier issued by the authorising master system; agent id is a foreign key.

layers.name: Policy, guardrails and threat posture
layers.description: Standing constraints, safety policies and agentic threat controls that apply to the actor across runs.

findings.name: Policy, guardrails and threat posture
findings.description: MCP treats tools as arbitrary code execution requiring consent, input validation, access control, rate limits and audit. OWASP documents agentic threats including memory poisoning, goal manipulation and tool misuse. Policies here are agent-standing controls, not run logs.

questions.text: Which standing policy packs, guardrails and deny-lists apply to this agent regardless of the current run?
Which agentic threats (memory poisoning, goal manipulation, tool misuse and related ASI items) have been assessed for this agent, and which mitigations are in force?
How are policy refusals, unauthorised function requests and internal failures represented, and who is notified?
Which personal or confidential data classes may the agent process, and which sharing destinations are forbidden without consent?

data_elements.name: Policy pack references
data_elements.description: Standing policy and guardrail packs bound to the agent.

data_elements.name: Assessed threat identifiers
data_elements.description: OWASP agentic threat identifiers covered for this agent.

data_elements.name: Permitted data classes
data_elements.description: Data classes the agent may process under its mandate.

artifacts.name: Agent policy pack
artifacts.description: Versioned set of guardrails, deny-lists, threat mitigations and privacy constraints.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by policy pack identifier and version; bound to agent master-system id.

bundles.name: Skills, tools and memory
bundles.description: What the agent can do, which tools and resources it may invoke, and how it retains context across time, without collapsing tools into runs or prompts.
bundles.rationale: A2A skills describe advertised capabilities to peers while keeping tools opaque; MCP makes tools, resources and prompts explicit to a host; OWASP treats memory and tool use as attack surfaces; NIST treats tool availability and context compression as scaffolding settings.

layers.name: Skills and tool bindings
layers.description: Advertised skills versus invocable tools and resources, including schemas, safety annotations and change notification.

findings.name: Skill catalog
findings.description: An A2A AgentSkill has an id, name, description, tags and examples and is the peer-visible capability unit. FIPA service-description similarly records name, type, protocols, ontologies, languages, ownership and properties. Skills are not prompts (WM-AI-005) and not runs.

questions.text: Which skills does this agent advertise, and what identifiers, tags and examples describe each skill?
Where did each skill originate (first-party, registry, third-party pack), and which version is pinned?
Which skills are public, which appear only on an extended card, and which principals may invoke each skill?

data_elements.name: Skills
data_elements.description: Collection of skill objects with id, name, description, tags and examples.

data_elements.name: Service types
data_elements.description: FIPA service-description type values, including reserved fipa-df and fipa-ams.

artifacts.name: Skill catalog
artifacts.description: Versioned catalog of advertised skills and service descriptions.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Each skill keyed by skill id unique within the agent; catalog versioned with the discovery manifest.

findings.name: Tool and resource bindings
findings.description: MCP tools are model-controlled functions with unique names, input and optional output schemas. Hosts should obtain consent, treat annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted, validate inputs, rate-limit, sanitize outputs and log use. A2A peers do not receive internal tool implementations. Tool calls during a run belong to WM-AI-004; this finding records the standing binding set.

questions.text: Which tools and resources are bound to this agent, and what names, titles, descriptions and schemas define them?
For each tool, is user consent required before invocation, and are tool annotations treated as untrusted?
What validation, rate limits, timeouts, output sanitization and audit logging are required for tool calls by this agent?
May the tool list change over time, and how are list-changed notifications handled without per-connection variance except by authorization?

data_elements.name: Tool bindings
data_elements.description: Standing set of tools the agent may invoke, each with name and schemas.

data_elements.name: Resource bindings
data_elements.description: URI-identified resources available as context to the agent.

data_elements.name: Tool consent map
data_elements.description: Per-tool consent and human-denial requirements.

artifacts.name: Agent tool registry
artifacts.description: Inventory of bound tools and resources with schemas and safety metadata.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Tool names unique per server; aggregated inventories must disambiguate across servers and must not use non-unique server display names as the only key.

layers.name: Memory and context architecture
layers.description: Standing memory stores, context-compression facilities and retention of conversational or working context at agent grain.

findings.name: Memory and context architecture
findings.description: No ISO or FIPA schema defines LLM-agent memory. OWASP treats short- and long-term memory poisoning as an agentic threat. NIST records context-compression tools and agent budgets as scaffolding that let an agent operate past ordinary context limits. A2A keeps internal memory opaque to peers. This finding records the architecture, integrity controls and retention of agent memory, not the contents of a run transcript.

questions.text: Which working, episodic and long-term memory stores does this agent use, and what integrity or isolation controls protect them against poisoning?
Does scaffolding provide context-compression or unbounded-horizon memory, and what stopping condition still applies?
How long may each memory class be retained, and who may inspect, correct or erase it?
Is internal memory hidden from peer agents under opaque execution, and which summaries if any may be exported?

data_elements.name: Memory stores
data_elements.description: Declared memory stores and their kinds.

data_elements.name: Context-compression flag
data_elements.description: Whether the agent scaffolding provides context compression beyond the model context window.

data_elements.name: Memory retention rules
data_elements.description: Retention and erasure rules by memory class.

artifacts.name: Memory architecture map
artifacts.description: Description of stores, isolation, integrity controls, compression and retention. Contents of stores are not this artifact.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by agent master-system id plus architecture version.

bundles.name: Lifecycle, directory and scaffolding
bundles.description: How an agent is created, registered, suspended, moved, evaluated for readiness, budgeted and retired on a platform, distinct from the lifecycle of a task or run.
bundles.rationale: FIPA defines an application-independent, instance-oriented, unique platform lifecycle with AMS-enforced transitions, directory registration and optional lease times. NIST requires explicit agent budgets and stopping conditions. AWS-style operational decommission is an industry practice, not a substitute for FIPA states.

layers.name: Platform lifecycle state
layers.description: FIPA states initiated, active, suspended, waiting, transit and unknown, with transitions create, invoke, destroy, quit, suspend, resume, wait, wake, move and execute. Only mobile agents enter transit. Message delivery behaviour depends on state.

findings.name: Agent platform lifecycle
findings.description: Each agent has exactly one AP life-cycle state at a time on one platform. AMS maintains the state, may force destroy, and buffers or forwards messages in non-active states. This is not the A2A TaskState machine.

questions.text: What is this agent's current platform lifecycle state, and on which agent platform does that state apply?
Which lifecycle transitions are allowed from the current state, and which actors (agent versus AMS) may initiate each transition?
At what event time did the current state begin, and at what observation or ingestion time was that transition recorded?
In the current state, does the message transport buffer, forward or reject inbound messages?

data_elements.name: Lifecycle state
data_elements.description: FIPA AP state: initiated, active, suspended, waiting, transit, or unknown.

data_elements.name: Agent platform identifier
data_elements.description: Platform to which this lifecycle instance is bound.

data_elements.name: Mobility supported
data_elements.description: Whether the agent may enter transit and move between platforms.

data_elements.name: State event time
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 event time of the last lifecycle transition.

artifacts.name: Lifecycle transition log
artifacts.description: Append-only record of state transitions with initiator, event time and ingestion time.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Each transition keyed by agent master-system id plus unique transition id; not by date.

layers.name: Registration, lease, scaffolding and retirement
layers.description: Directory registration, lease times, how a model is turned into an agent, budgets, and decommission.

findings.name: Directory registration and lease
findings.description: An agent must register with the AMS of its home platform to obtain a valid AID. DF registration advertises services and may carry a lease time after which the DF may silently remove the entry. Register, deregister, modify and search are the management functions.

questions.text: Is this agent registered with its home AMS, and which ams-agent-description (name, ownership, state) is stored?
Which Directory Facilitators hold a description of this agent, and when does each registration lease expire or renew?
What search constraints, access restrictions and exception codes apply when other agents look up this agent?

data_elements.name: AMS registered flag
data_elements.description: Whether the agent currently holds an AMS registration on its HAP.

data_elements.name: Directory lease time
data_elements.description: Duration or absolute expiry of DF registration; unlimited if omitted by a DF that does not support leases.

data_elements.name: AMS ownership string
data_elements.description: Owner recorded on the ams-agent-description.

artifacts.name: Directory agent description
artifacts.description: AMS and/or DF description records for this agent, including lease metadata.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by AID name on the issuing AMS or DF; lease expiry is metadata, not identity.

findings.name: Scaffolding, budget and decommission
findings.description: NIST defines agent scaffolding as exactly how a model is turned into an agent (ReAct-style loops or pre-built agent products) and requires an explicit agent budget and stopping condition because agents can run for an extended or indefinite period. Decommission must remove directory entries, mandates, tools and memory per FIPA deregistration and OWASP governance of autonomy. Inference settings of the underlying model are referenced, not copied from a model card.

questions.text: Which scaffolding pattern or pre-built agent product turns the backing model into this agent, and which tools does that scaffolding expose?
What standing budget and stopping condition limit this agent's runtime (tokens, wall-clock, step count), and who may raise the budget?
What residual registrations, mandates, tools, memory and credentials must be removed when the agent is destroyed or quits, and who attests completeness?

data_elements.name: Scaffolding descriptor
data_elements.description: Pattern or product used to wrap the model as an agent.

data_elements.name: Agent budget
data_elements.description: Standing runtime budget and unit.

data_elements.name: Stopping condition
data_elements.description: Explicit condition that ends an otherwise unbounded agentic loop.

artifacts.name: Scaffolding and budget profile
artifacts.description: Record of how the model is agentified, tool availability, budget and stopping condition.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by agent master-system id plus scaffolding profile version.

bundles.name: Relationships and interoperability
bundles.description: How this agent is composed with systems, persons, prompts, runs and peer agents, and which communication protocols it speaks.
bundles.rationale: Known Vercy relations compose agents under AI systems, reference prompts, and have runs point at executing agents. FIPA ACL and A2A provide incompatible but alignable conversation models; MCP is a host-to-tool protocol, not an agent-to-agent protocol.

layers.name: System, principal and peer composition
layers.description: Typed links from this agent to its parent system, owning person, instruction configuration, and other agents.

findings.name: Composition and relationship links
findings.description: An agent combines service capabilities into one execution model on a platform. It must have at least one owner. It may be one of several actors exposed by an AI system. Peer collaboration in A2A is capability-based and must not require shared internal state. Conversation-id in FIPA ACL groups communicative acts; A2A contextId groups tasks and messages. Those conversation instances belong to WM-AI-004 but the allowed peer set belongs here.

questions.text: Which AI system exposes this agent, and is the agent required to exist only inside that system?
Which person or organisation owns this agent, and are additional owners recorded?
Which prompt or agent-configuration artifacts does this agent currently use?
Which peer agents may this agent discover, delegate to or refuse, and is internal state shared with them?

data_elements.name: Parent AI system reference
data_elements.description: WM-AI-001 instance that exposes this actor.

data_elements.name: Owner references
data_elements.description: One or more owners as required by FIPA.

data_elements.name: Instruction configuration references
data_elements.description: Links to WM-AI-005 prompt or configuration artifacts.

data_elements.name: Peer allowlist
data_elements.description: Peer agents this agent may contact.

artifacts.name: Typed relationship set
artifacts.description: Set of typed edges from this agent to systems, persons, configurations, tools and peers.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Each edge keyed by source agent id, relation type and target id.

layers.name: Communication and tool protocol alignment
layers.description: Alignments to FIPA ACL, A2A and MCP without claiming mutual conformance.

findings.name: Communication protocol profiles
findings.description: FIPA ACL messages require a performative and typically sender, receiver and content, with conversation-id globally unique when a protocol is used. A2A uses messages with roles user/agent, parts, and task-centric operations over JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP/REST, and treats execution as opaque. MCP uses JSON-RPC between hosts, clients and servers for tools, resources and prompts. An agent may speak one or more of these; encodings are projections.

questions.text: Which inter-agent and tool protocols does this agent speak, and which protocol versions are declared?
How does this agent mint or accept conversation, context and message identifiers so concurrent dialogues stay distinct?
Does this agent refuse to expose internal plans, memory or tool implementations to A2A peers while still exposing MCP tools to its host?
In which jurisdictions or processing locations may this agent run or persist data, given EU territorial scope for AI systems used in the Union?

data_elements.name: Spoken protocol set
data_elements.description: Declared protocols and versions.

data_elements.name: Conversation identifier strategy
data_elements.description: How globally unique conversation identifiers are formed.

data_elements.name: Processing regions
data_elements.description: Jurisdictions or locations where the agent may execute or store data.

artifacts.name: Protocol alignment profile
artifacts.description: Declared protocol support, identifier strategies, opacity rules and residency.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by agent master-system id plus profile version.

bundles.name: Governance, access and evidence
bundles.description: Who is legally and operationally accountable, who may read or change the agent record, how long records persist, and what evaluation evidence supports continued operation.
bundles.rationale: EU AI Act duties attach to providers and deployers of autonomous systems. FIPA AMS is the managing authority of a platform. NIST 800-2 requires documented scaffolding and budgets for reproducible agent evaluation. OWASP requires threat assessment of autonomous actors.

layers.name: Legal roles, access, audit and retention
layers.description: Provider, deployer, owner, AMS authority, access scopes, audit and deletion.

findings.name: Ownership, legal roles, access and retention
findings.description: The EU AI Act defines providers who place AI systems on the market or into service and deployers who use them under their authority; agents inherit those roles through the system they instantiate. FIPA AMS exerts supervisory control, can refuse unauthorised management actions, and can forcibly destroy an agent. Access to directory data may be restricted. Retention of agent records, memory and logs must be explicit because silent DF lease expiry is not a substitute for governed deletion.

questions.text: Who is the provider and who is the deployer of the AI system that exposes this agent, and who is the FIPA owner?
Who may read, modify, suspend or destroy this agent record at bundle, layer, finding and artifact scope, and which actions are refused as unauthorised?
Which management actions, tool consents and authority changes must be audited, and for how long?
When and how is the agent record, memory, directory entry and mandate deleted or anonymised, including after lease expiry or destroy?

data_elements.name: Provider identifier
data_elements.description: EU AI Act provider of the exposing system.

data_elements.name: Deployer identifier
data_elements.description: EU AI Act deployer using the system under its authority.

data_elements.name: Record access policy
data_elements.description: Roles permitted to read, modify, suspend or destroy.

data_elements.name: Retention and deletion policy
data_elements.description: Retention periods and deletion method for the agent record and related stores.

artifacts.name: Accountability and access record
artifacts.description: Provider, deployer, owner, access policy, audit and retention settings.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by agent master-system id plus governance version.

layers.name: Evaluation, quality and provenance
layers.description: How the agent is measured, what evidence supports claims, and how scaffolding settings are reported.

findings.name: Evaluation, provenance and quality evidence
findings.description: NIST AI 800-2 requires evaluations of agent systems to report scaffolding, tool availability, aggregation strategies, agent budget and stopping conditions separately from model inference settings. Quality claims without those settings are not comparable. OWASP assessments provide threat-coverage evidence. Provenance covers who created the agent, from which product or scaffold, and which measurements were observed.

questions.text: Which inference, scaffolding and task settings were used in the latest evaluation of this agent, and are they sufficient to reproduce the result?
What quality, safety or threat-coverage claims are made for this agent, and which artefacts or probe results support them?
What validation status does this agent currently hold (unevaluated, draft, passed, failed, waived), and who attested it?
Who created or imported this agent record, from which source system, and at what event versus ingestion times?

data_elements.name: Evaluation settings
data_elements.description: Inference, scaffolding and task settings per NIST AI 800-2.

data_elements.name: Validation status
data_elements.description: Current evaluation or assurance status of the agent.

data_elements.name: Provenance block
data_elements.description: Creator, source system, event time and ingestion time.

artifacts.name: Agent evaluation report
artifacts.description: Report of benchmark or probe results with scaffolding, budget, stopping condition and threat coverage.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by evaluation report identifier issued by the evaluating system; agent id is a foreign key.

functions.name: Register agent
functions.description: Register a new agent with the AMS and optionally a DF, issuing or confirming a master-system AID and initial lifecycle state.
inputs: ams-agent-description or equivalent identity and ownership payload
outputs: registered agent record with master-system identifier
preconditions: Caller is authorised by the AMS
AID name is unique on the home platform
At least one owner is present
effects: Agent becomes searchable on the platform
Lifecycle state is initiated or active
Lease clock starts if a DF lease is accepted

functions.name: Deregister agent
functions.description: Remove AMS and DF descriptions so the AID can be released and message delivery no longer targets the agent.
preconditions: Agent is registered
Caller is authorised or is the AMS enforcing destroy
effects: Directory entries are removed
Further search no longer returns the agent
AID may be reused only according to platform policy

functions.name: Modify agent description
functions.description: Replace directory description parameters other than the immutable AID name, including addresses, services, ownership string and state.
preconditions: Agent is registered
Name parameter is unchanged
Caller is authorised
effects: Directory view changes
Lease may be renewed or shortened

functions.name: Search agent directory
functions.description: Query AMS white pages or DF yellow pages with a partial description template and search constraints.
preconditions: Caller is permitted to see matching entries
effects: No state change; may federate to other DFs when max-depth allows

functions.name: Publish discovery card
functions.description: Publish or rotate the public and optional extended Agent Card, including skills, interfaces and security schemes.
preconditions: Agent has a master-system identifier
Security schemes are valid for the advertised interfaces
effects: Peers can discover the agent
Capability validation thereafter uses the published card

functions.name: Bind or unbind tools
functions.description: Attach or detach MCP tools and resources to the agent's standing inventory, with consent and schema validation requirements.
preconditions: Caller is authorised
Tool names satisfy uniqueness and safety constraints
User consent policy is defined for newly bound tools
effects: Standing tool set changes
Subsequent runs see the new inventory
Audit log records the change

functions.name: Grant or revoke authority
functions.description: Create, suspend or revoke a delegation mandate that defines principal, scopes, limits and human-denial rules.
preconditions: Principal is authorised to delegate
Agent exists
Scopes are within the deployer's authority
effects: Agent may or may no longer act in the granted scopes
Authority event is audited with event and ingestion times

functions.name: Transition lifecycle state
functions.description: Apply a FIPA lifecycle transition (invoke, suspend, resume, wait, wake, move, execute, quit or destroy) and adjust message-delivery policy.
preconditions: Transition is legal from the current state
Destroy and resume are AMS-only as specified
Move is only for mobile agents
effects: Exactly one platform state is held
Messages are buffered, forwarded or delivered according to the new state

functions.name: Evaluate agent
functions.description: Run or record an automated benchmark or threat assessment that captures scaffolding, budget, stopping condition and threat coverage.
preconditions: Settings distinguish inference, scaffolding and task factors
Stopping condition is explicit
effects: Validation status changes
Evidence artifact is attached to the agent

functions.name: Decommission agent
functions.description: Gracefully quit or forcibly destroy the agent and remove residual directory entries, mandates, tool credentials and memory according to retention policy.
preconditions: Caller is AMS or an authorised deployer
Legal hold is not set, or destroy is still legally permitted
effects: Agent is not active
Registrations, mandates and credentials are removed or sealed
Retention schedule for logs and evidence continues independently

composition.purpose: Identify the engineered AI system that exposes this agent actor; system-level lifecycle, models and risk management stay on WM-AI-001.
Point at operational instruction and configuration artifacts used by this agent without treating those artifacts as the agent.
Allow lookup of execution records that cite this agent; run and A2A Task state machines are not stored here.
Record the required owner or principal; the agent does not acquire legal personality.
Align the actor type to the ISO definition of an AI agent as an automated entity that senses, responds and acts toward goals.
Align identity, ownership, directory, lifecycle and communicative-act parameters without claiming a FIPA-compliant implementation.

composition.target: A2A Protocol 1.0 Agent Card and skills
composition.purpose: Align discovery, skills, interfaces and opaque peer execution with the Linux Foundation A2A specification.

composition.target: Model Context Protocol tools and resources
composition.purpose: Align standing tool and resource bindings, consent and human denial with MCP, which is a host-tool protocol rather than an agent-agent protocol.
Align accountability fields to EU provider and deployer duties for autonomous AI systems; do not invent an EU 'AI agent' legal class.

owner_package_requirements: Name an accountable deployer and, where the EU AI Act applies, the provider of the exposing AI system.
Name at least one owner principal as required by FIPA agent management.
Declare the home agent platform or master system that issues the authoritative agent identifier.
Publish specification, storage-type, interface and process URLs in AGENTS.md before the Dimension accepts writes.
dimension.namespace_guidance: Use a Dimension namespace under NAV.INF.AI.AGT keyed by the master-system agent identifier. Do not use dates as identifiers. Protocol locators (well-known Agent Card URLs, MCP server names, DF addresses) are aliases, not namespace roots.

canonicalization_rules: Canonical identity is the master-system AID name; display names and locators are non-identifying.
Two records with the same AID name are the same agent; merge aliases rather than duplicating.
Protocol-specific encodings (JSON Agent Cards, protobuf, FIPA-SL, MCP JSON-RPC) canonicalise to the same actor fields.
Timestamps canonicalise to RFC 3339 with seconds and a numeric offset or Z.
patch_rules: Patches may not change the master-system identifier.
Lifecycle transitions must be applied as whole transitions with initiator, not as free edits of the state field.
Skill, tool and policy patches increment the corresponding artifact serial and record provenance.
Unauthorised modify requests are refused rather than partially applied.
compatibility_rules: A2A 0.3 and 1.0 interface shapes are stored as alignments; do not silently drop tenant or supportedInterfaces.
MCP tool name uniqueness is per server; aggregations must disambiguate.
FIPA optional parameters omitted by one party are not inferred as protocol agreement with another party.
Claiming FIPA, A2A, MCP or EU AI Act conformance requires explicit evidence artefacts; alignment is the default.

identity_priority: Authoritative master-system identifier issued by the Agent Management System or home agent platform (FIPA AID name parameter)
Governed global identifier or IRI such as a published Agent Card locator or well-known agent URI
UUID or ULID assigned by the adopting Dimension when no master-system or global identifier exists
artifact_rules.timestamp_rule: All agent-related times SHALL be recorded as RFC 3339 timestamps including seconds and an explicit offset or Z. Record the event time of a lifecycle, authority, registration, communication or evaluation occurrence separately from the observation or ingestion time at which the Dimension received or recorded it whenever those differ.
artifact_rules.serial_naming_rule: Serial artifacts use the pattern <artifact-kind>-<master-system-agent-id>-v<monotonic-integer> without embedding calendar dates in the identifier.
artifact_rules.integrity_rule: Serial artifacts carry a content digest and provenance (author, source system, event time, ingestion time). Tool annotations and unauthenticated discovery cards are marked untrusted until a trusted source or extended-card authentication is recorded.

policies: Least privilege on tools, directory data and extended Agent Cards; undeclared A2A capabilities must be rejected.
Human consent and a denial path are required before invoking tools that execute code or exfiltrate data.
Goal, mandate and policy changes are audited and cannot be performed by the agent on its own standing charter without an authorised principal.
No conformance claim to ISO, FIPA, A2A, MCP or the EU AI Act without linked evidence.
Memory stores are integrity-protected against poisoning and are opaque to A2A peers by default.

read: Authenticated callers may read fields allowed by their role at bundle, layer, finding or artifact scope.
Extended discovery data is returned only after a declared security scheme succeeds.
Directory search returns only entries the caller is authorised to see; absence and unauthorised must not be distinguishable where FIPA/A2A anti-leakage applies.
create: Create requires an owner, a master-system identifier or a request for the AMS to issue one, and AGENTS.md bootstrap URLs for the Dimension package.
Register is refused if the AID is already registered.
Initial lifecycle state and mandate must be set in the same authorised transaction or explicitly deferred.
update: Updates use modify semantics: replacement descriptions must include a valid AID and must not rename the agent.
Lifecycle, mandate and tool-inventory updates are transition functions, not blind field writes.
Patch provenance and serial increments are mandatory for policy, skill and scaffolding artifacts.
delete: Delete is deregister, quit or AMS destroy followed by governed retention of logs and evaluation evidence.
DF lease expiry may silently remove a yellow-pages entry but does not by itself destroy the agent or its audit trail.
Legal hold blocks erasure of accountability and evaluation artifacts.

roles.name: Deployer (accountable operator)
responsibilities: Put the exposing AI system and this agent into service under its authority
Maintain policy packs, access control and retention
Ensure human denial paths exist for tool use

roles.name: Provider
responsibilities: Where the EU AI Act applies, remain responsible for the exposing AI system placed on the market or put into service
Supply documentation that the deployer can apply to this agent instance

roles.name: Platform AMS operator
responsibilities: Enforce register, modify, search and lifecycle transitions

roles.name: Security and evaluation reviewer
responsibilities: Attest NIST-style scaffolding, budget and stopping conditions
Mark discovery cards and tool annotations trusted or untrusted

access.default_rule: Deny read and write of agent records, extended cards, memory maps, mandates and tool registries unless the caller is the owner, deployer, AMS operator or a role explicitly granted a scope.
exceptions: Public discovery fields on a published Agent Card or DF description are readable without authentication when the publisher marked them public.
AMS may read and destroy any resident agent for platform safety.
Break-glass access by a security reviewer is allowed for incident response and must be audited.
audit_requirements: Record actor, action, target scope, outcome, event time and ingestion time for register, modify, lifecycle, mandate, tool-bind, evaluate and decommission.
Retain audit records independently of DF leases and of agent destroy, for the stated retention period or legal hold.

coverage.claim: This research defines a format-neutral AI Agent entity as the defensible union of ISO/IEC 22989's agent concept, FIPA identity/lifecycle/directory/ownership, A2A discovery and skills, MCP tool bindings, EU AI Act provider/deployer accountability, NIST agent scaffolding and budgets, and OWASP agentic threat surfaces. It is an alignment model, not a claim that any implementation conforms to all of those instruments.

checklist.notes: FIPA AID name as master-system identifier; A2A display name/version and well-known locators as aliases; Dimension UUID/ULID as last resort.
FIPA platform states and transitions plus registration, lease, quit/destroy and decommission; A2A TaskState explicitly excluded as run-level.
Links to WM-AI-001, WM-AI-005, WM-AI-004, WM-PER-003, peers, tools and skills.
RFC 3339 event versus ingestion times on lifecycle, mandate, lease and evaluation; agent budget as a duration limit.
Creation source, skill supply chain, evaluation settings and serial artifact digests.
FIPA mandatory owner plus EU provider and deployer roles; agent is not a legal person.
NIST scaffolding/budget/stopping-condition reporting and validation status on the agent record.
AMS authorisation, public versus extended Agent Cards, directory visibility, tool consent and scoped CRUD.
DF lease expiry versus governed destroy; memory and audit retention; legal hold.
Alignments to FIPA ACL, A2A 1.0 and MCP 2026-07-28 with explicit non-conformance default and opacity rules.
Mandates, permission scopes, human denial of tool calls, standing goals and OWASP goal-manipulation controls.
Standing MCP tool/resource bindings and memory architecture; run transcripts remain WM-AI-004.

known_omissions: No primary ISO or IEC schema for LLM long-term memory, episodic memory or memory-poisoning mitigations beyond OWASP threat language.
IETF and community drafts (AID DNS discovery, SAMP, A2A WebFinger) are emerging and not treated as canonical.
NIST CAISI AI Agent Standards Initiative (announced 2026-02-17) has not yet issued a durable identity or authorization standard; this model should be revisited when those deliverables appear.
OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 and payment/mandate protocols (for example AP2 or x402) lack sufficient primary, multi-organisation backing in the sources fetched for this run.
Physical embodiment, swarm orchestration topologies and agent legal personhood are out of scope or unsupported.
ISO/IEC 42001 AI management systems and ISO/IEC 23894 risk management apply to organisations and systems, not to a single agent record, and were not inlined.
conflicts: FIPA AID (immutable name plus addresses/resolvers) versus A2A Agent Card (name, version, supportedInterfaces) versus MCP serverInfo: three identity surfaces, none globally authoritative across ecosystems.
FIPA requires at least one owner; A2A provider is optional; EU duties attach to providers and deployers of AI systems, not to 'agents'.
A2A opaque execution hides tools and memory from peers; MCP requires tools to be explicit to the host: both can be true of one agent but must not be collapsed.
FIPA lifecycle (initiated/active/suspended/waiting/transit) is not the A2A TaskState machine (SUBMITTED/WORKING/COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELED/REJECTED/INPUT_REQUIRED/AUTH_REQUIRED).
ISO/IEC 22989 'AI agent' is a concept; the EU AI Act regulates 'AI systems' with autonomy. Claiming that every ISO agent is an EU AI system, or that the Act defines agents, is a category error.
regional_assumptions: EU provider/deployer fields are required in substance only when the exposing system is in territorial scope of Regulation 2024/1689.
FIPA AMS/DF patterns remain normative in some industrial multi-agent platforms and are treated as an alignment even where LLM-agent products do not implement them.
A2A well-known Agent Card discovery assumes internet or enterprise HTTP locators; offline or mesh agents need equivalent locators.
NIST AI 800-2 is an initial public draft of evaluation practice, not a binding US regulation.
adversarial_checks: Verified that A2A TaskState and run transcripts were not modelled as the agent lifecycle.
Verified that MCP, JSON, Git and MongoDB were treated as projections, not as the agent semantic.
Verified that ISO 22989, FIPA, A2A, MCP and the EU AI Act are recorded as ALIGN relations without a universal conformance claim.
Verified that owner/provider/deployer are persons or organisations (WM-PER-003 and legal entities), not the agent itself.
Verified that dates are not used as identifiers and that event time is separated from observation or ingestion time.
Marked memory schema, IETF drafts, CAISI future identity work and payment mandates as omissions rather than canonical nodes.
